book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

chapters.file: ch03 - Stranger Things and Philosophy Thus Spake the Demogorgon.md
ch09 - How to Make Something Strange Even Stranger.md
chapters.relation: Andrew Winters's introduction argues the show appeals both to those who lived the Eighties and those who wish they had: plastic, story-rich 1980s childhoods (D&D, bikes, walkie-talkies) versus a present of single-bit tweets, likes, and Instagram-filtered self-display where we look to others for confirmation instead of creating worlds together. It then previews the volume's essays on horror's appeal, whether monsters like Dart are all evil, friendship and civil disobedience, the Shadow Monster within ourselves, Will's possession and identity, nostalgia and forgetting, and Eleven's faith and heroism as a guide to meaningful living, closing with Hopper's 'Mornings are for coffee and contemplation.'

Holmes and Christensen read the #JusticeForBarb movement through Baudrillard's hyperreality: fans mobilized real activism for a fictional girl the show killed as a plot device (dragged by the Demogorgon while Nancy and Steve are upstairs), while real murdered women like Jamie Haggard got no hashtag, so fictional justice becomes 'more real than the real.' The show itself is a simulacrum assembled from 1980s movies (E.T., Poltergeist, Firestarter, The Goonies, Stand by Me) whose grid motif casts the series as a D&D gameboard the audience plays, and the chapter argues hyperreal power became real power when the Duffers gave Barb a Season Two funeral and apology from Hawkins Lab.

chapters.file: ch12 - 2. Can Anything Good Come from the Upside Down.md
chapters.relation: Kuzma maps Augustine's two cities onto the two Hawkinses: not two places but two mixed moral orientations in one world, since Will is literally 'right here' in the same house flipped upside down. Augustine's privation view of evil (evil as absence of good, a nougat-less Three Musketeers) explains how Dart can come from the 'evil' Upside Down yet love Dustin and let the party pass, while Brenner, from the right side up, is ruled by libido dominandi like the Mind Flayer and Dr. Owens proves Hawkins Lab is not automatically bad; it is how you act, not where you are from.

Puumala asks whether killing the Demogorgons is speciesist: Dart's pain response to light makes the demodogs sentient (Bentham's 'Can they suffer?'), giving them moral considerability, while the Mind Flayer may or may not be a moral agent and could even be a keystone species whose destruction collapses the Upside Down ecosystem. He tests whether demogorgons count as invasive species (they may be native to a causally connected mirror dimension), invokes Regan's lifeboat case to argue they must still lose out to humans in a conflict of interests, and ends with the uncomfortable thought that humans are themselves an invasive species turning Earth into an Upside Down, so Eleven closing the gate was compassionate conservation.

chapters.file: ch14 - II The Joy of the Creepy.md
ch15 - 4. The Slimy, Macabre, and Horrific in Stranger Things.md
chapters.relation: Nisley applies Noel Carroll's account of art-horror to the Demogorgon: categorically transgressive, interdimensional monsters provoke thought-based fear and disgust (the shed goop, the hazmat suits, Barb's blood in the pool), and it is precisely this disgust that makes our curiosity about the monster's origin and disclosure pleasurable. She traces Nancy's investigation from Jonathan's photograph to the bear trap, brings in Plato's Leontius story from the Republic and Kieran and Feagin on the grotesque to explain why we paradoxically delight in Barb's slime-covered corpse and Will coughing up a slug, and concludes that revulsion amplifies the fascination that keeps us watching.

chapters.file: ch16 - 5. Horror Appeals to Our Dual Nature.md
chapters.relation: Allaire and Gehring argue horror works on Kierkegaard's dual nature, the tug-of-war between finitude and infinitude that produces despair: the show's corporeal terrors (the Demogorgon's kills, Barb's decomposing body with a slug in its mouth, Will's tentacle) trigger the fear of mutilation and extinction, while the intelligent Shadow Monster shatters our sense of being unique, echoing Ernest Becker's claim that we build cultural 'armor' against mortality. Using Carroll's paradox of horror and Stephen King's three levels (revulsion, horror, terror), they contend we enjoy confronting these fears safely from the couch, with the Shadow Monster looming over the Snow Ball as an emblem of real horrors, from AIDS to 9/11, still to come.

chapters.file: ch17 - 6. The Unique Horror of the Upside Down.md
chapters.relation: Pamerleau argues the Upside Down's distinctive horror is not its monsters, which offer familiar Jaws-style jump scares and supervillain plots, but the place itself: reading Will through Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world, our selves are constituted by the web of socially inherited meanings (the 'they') attached to familiar places and things. Waking in a dead replica of home, where the same houses, school, and Castle Byers no longer function or answer back, forces Will to spell 'R-I-G-H-T H-E-R-E' through the lights, an uncanny juxtaposition of the familiar and the alien that the chapter compares to an open-casket funeral and contrasts with Alien's wholly unknown ship.

chapters.file: ch18 - III Nothing Is Stranger than Reality.md
ch19 - 7. The Mind Flayer through a Gnostic Lens.md
chapters.relation: Ewing reads the Mind Flayer as the Demiurge of the Upside Down, a dark derivative copy of our world complete with replicated Castle Byers and school decorations: he surveys Plato's Timaeus craftsman who shapes chaotic matter on the model of the Forms, Plotinus's One and its secondary demiurge, and the Gnostic variants, from the Valentinian just-but-imperfect craftsman to the Sethian Yaldabaoth, a serpent-faced false god who steals divine power. Because the Mind Flayer hive-minds Will and the demodogs, wants to conquer our dimension as a 'master race,' and hates the real world rather than serving it, the chapter concludes it matches the Sethian evil Demiurge, an incorporeal entity playing at being god.

Wigley uses Baudrillard's hyperreality and semiotics to argue that Eggos, not Eleven, are Hawkins's true savior: as Barb's Xeroxed missing-poster face drifts through generations of models away from the original photo, so Eggos accumulate new symbolic value as tokens of trust and friendship, from Mike's blanket-fort promise of 'as many Eggos as you want' to Hopper's box in the snow-covered woods that tells El she can come home. The Party's Dungeons & Dragons vocabulary (naming the Demogorgon, Dustin's 'best metaphor') is their shared code for making sense of a reality shattered by adolescence, Reagan-era image politics, and the Upside Down, and the trust the waffles symbolize extends past the screen to the viewer.

chapters.file: ch21 - 9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime.md
chapters.relation: Huntingford contrasts Stranger Things with its blueprint, Stephen King's It: where It forces the Losers Club back to the traumatic truth of childhood, the show traffics in 'false nostalgia,' vicarious nostalgia for an Eighties that only existed on screen, supported by Loftus's false-memory experiments (the impossible Bugs Bunny, Stewart's Root Beer) and Will's anniversary effect and El's mother's broken record of 'breathe, sunflower, rainbow... 450.' Against this malleability she sets Locke's memory theory of personal identity from the Essay and Sacks's 'lost mariner,' warning that nostalgic self-deception can rewrite the self, yet concluding, with It's own ending, that since we cannot survive some horrors, the comforting lie of misremembered childhood is what we tune in for.

chapters.file: ch22 - IV How Strange Are We.md

chapters.relation: Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'

Zanin applies Foucault's Abnormal lectures, where a monster is a juridico-natural being violating both the laws of nature and of society, to the show: the Demogorgon and demodogs break biology and morality, while El and Eight are biologically abnormal (psionic) and law-breaking, making them Foucauldian monsters too, as Lucas's 'maybe she's the monster?' suggests. Monsters emerge wherever power/knowledge assemblages operate, hence Hawkins Lab's MK-Ultra-style experimentation conjuring the very Demogorgon it hunts, and the chapter extends monstrosity to human 'assholes' like Brenner, Lonnie, and Billy before concluding that knowing the monster, being a freak, is a virtue and a weapon against fear.

Hammonds and Gordon use Mead's symbolic interactionism, in which the self emerges from interaction and stabilizes around 'identity anchors' others can expect, to unpack 'Zombie Boy': Mr. Clarke's Phineas Gage story frames Max's doubt that Will is still Will, Joyce's hovering and Will's fragile-child role co-constitute each other, and Will renegotiates a different identity with Jonathan ('Stop treating me like I'm gonna break'). During the Mind Flayer's possession, when Will screams that the creature is 'everywhere,' his family's stories of the toy truck and the crayon spaceship summon the kind, honest anchors of the old Will, showing identity as recognizable and stable yet ultimately negotiable, and that realizing and actualizing agency lets Will beat the role the monster assigned him.

chapters.file: ch26 - V How Do We Cope with the Strange.md

chapters.relation: Guerra and Barkman argue the Party and Hopper practice Thoreauvian civil disobedience: the boys sneak out at night despite Hopper's explicit order, Hopper breaks into Hawkins Lab twice and exposes the fake body in the quarry, and the kids steal Billy's car to reach Will because 'a Party member requires assistance.' They accept Thoreau's point that disobeying unjust laws is right even at great risk, then distill three tests from the show for when laws should be broken: laws made with bad intent (the Lab's secrecy and human experimentation), laws contradicted by new knowledge (anything ignoring the Upside Down), and laws that block a greater good (speeding to save a dying stranger, trespassing to save Will).

Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.

chapters.file: ch29 - 15. Abnormal Is the New Normal.md
chapters.relation: Berns, Foronda, and Zarate read the show anachronistically (via Didi-Huberman), arguing its millennial sensibilities deliberately clash with the 1980s setting to reveal that normalcy is a shifting social discourse rather than a natural fact: Joyce defends Will's possible sexuality like no 1980s mother would, Jonathan claims freakishness as a right, and audiences mourn plain, awkward Barb. Through Foucault's three figures from Abnormal, the monster (androgynous, tomboy-coded Eleven called 'freak'), the individual to be corrected (hippie Terry Ives, 'hysterical' Joyce, un-macho boys), and the masturbator (surveillance of the most intimate life), plus biopolitics and bullying as State-sanctioned discipline, they show the abnormal are the heroes: 'The X-Men are weirdos.'

Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.

holes.name: Art-Horror (the paradox of horror)
holes.what: Noel Carroll's account of horror fiction: categorically transgressive, interstitial monsters produce art-horror through thought-based fear and disgust, and curiosity about them yields a paradoxical pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire explanation of the Demogorgon's appeal on Carroll's art-horror (with Kieran and Feagin on the grotesque), and chapters 16-17 reuse it; no taxonomy slug covers philosophy of horror.

holes.name: Terror Management (the denial of death)
holes.what: Ernest Becker's thesis that humans, uniquely aware of their mortality, build cultural and symbolic 'armor' (flags, religion, teams) to buffer the anxiety of death.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Becker's Denial of Death alongside Kierkegaard to explain why we seek out horror from a position of safety and why the Shadow Monster terrifies.

holes.name: The Demiurge (Gnosticism)
holes.what: A craftsman-creator entity, from Plato's Timaeus through Plotinus and the Gnostics, who fashions the material world as an imperfect copy of ultimate reality; for Sethian Gnostics an evil false god (Yaldabaoth).
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole reading of the Mind Flayer as ruler of the Upside Down works by comparing Plato's, Plotinus's, and the Sethian Gnostic versions of the Demiurge, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: The Monster and the Abnormal (Abnormal lectures)
holes.what: Foucault's account of the juridico-natural monster (violating laws of nature and society) and the three figures, monster, individual to be corrected, masturbator, from which the modern 'abnormal' is produced via normalization.
holes.why: Chapter 24 defines every monster in the show through this framework, and no taxonomy slug captures Foucault's monster/abnormality analysis distinct from power-knowledge.

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist social philosopher whose symbolic interactionism holds that the self emerges from social interaction through shared symbols and stable 'identity anchors.'
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire account of Will Byers's identity before, during, and after Mind Flayer possession is built on Mead's symbolic interactionism, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: The Monster and the Abnormal (Abnormal lectures)
holes.what: Foucault's account of the juridico-natural monster and the three figures (monster, individual to be corrected, masturbator) from which the modern 'abnormal' is produced through normalization and biopolitics.
holes.why: Chapter 29 structures its whole reading of freaks, tomboys, and 1980s normalcy around the three figures from Foucault's Abnormal, the same gap as chapter 24.
